title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
gist: An MIT-led Nature study (Jevan Yu et al.) estimates historical peatland drainage accounts for about 2.7% (1.8-3.6%) of human-caused radiative forcing as of 2020, with +83 mW/m2 from CO2 partly offset by -9 mW/m2 from reduced methane. Drained peat keeps emitting: holding water levels constant nearly doubles the forcing to 138 mW/m2 by 2100, while ambitious rewetting could push it below 2020 levels.

insights.claim: Peatlands hold about 600 billion tons of carbon, more than all of the world's living vegetation.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Peatland preservation and rewetting is a large-scale lever for nature-based carbon markets.
insights.locator: A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT

insights.claim: Draining peatlands for agriculture lowers the water table, letting aerobic bacteria decompose the peat, which sharply raises CO2 emissions while reducing methane emissions from anaerobic decay.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Agricultural land conversion carries an ongoing emissions liability that carbon accounting and offset schemes can price.
insights.quote: Methane emissions get turned down, and CO2 emissions get turned way up.
insights.locator: Many peatlands have been drained by digging ditches

insights.claim: Land-use change accounts for about one-third of total historical human CO2 emissions, with deforestation and wetland drainage the major contributors.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Climate policy focused only on fossil fuels misses a large share of emissions addressable through land management.
insights.locator: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change

insights.claim: Historical peatland drainage produced about +83 mW/m2 of radiative forcing from CO2 and -9 mW/m2 from reduced methane by 2020, a net +73 mW/m2 equal to 2.7% (range 1.8-3.6%) of total human-caused change in Earth's energy budget.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Quantifies peatland drainage as a material, low-single-digit share of warming, supporting peat-restoration carbon credit methodologies.
insights.locator: The simplest way to represent the climate impact

insights.claim: Roughly 4 percent of all the carbon historically buried in peatlands is now in the atmosphere due to drainage.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Most peat carbon remains stored, so protecting undrained peat has large avoided-emissions value.
insights.locator: Or to look at it another way

insights.claim: Over half of peatland-drainage CO2 came from Europe, almost a quarter from Southeast Asia and only 14 percent from North America, with Southeast Asia's contribution surging only in the last few decades.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Southeast Asian peat drainage (e.g., for plantation agriculture) is the fast-growing source and a likely focus for regulation and offset projects.
insights.locator: Regionally, over half of the total CO2

insights.claim: Because drained peat keeps releasing carbon, holding peatland water levels constant from 2020 would nearly double their warming effect from 73 to 138 mW/m2 by 2100.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Past land-use decisions lock in decades of future emissions, increasing the long-run value of rewetting interventions.
insights.locator: If peatland water levels were simply held constant

insights.claim: Moderate peatland rewetting would slow the growth of drainage-driven warming, and ambitious restoration could shrink it slightly below its 2020 level by 2100, though a full return to 1800 landscapes is unlikely.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Peatland restoration is a scalable, policy-dependent mitigation pathway relevant to nature-based carbon credit demand.
insights.quote: This is a process we can halt if we really want to.
insights.locator: If peatland water levels were simply held constant
